en: Homage to the Triple Gem.
Having prostrated before the Omniscient One, who is liberated from all faults, adorned with all virtues, and the sole kinsman of all sentient beings,
I shall [speak] for you, O King, the Dharma that is exclusively auspicious, for the arising of Dharma.

I shall explain [the Dharma], for indeed the Dharma attains success when it resides in a vessel of the true Dharma. First there is the arising of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), and subsequently the arising of the ultimate good (*naiḥśreyasa*);
because, having attained prosperity, one reaches the ultimate good through gradual stages.
Happiness is considered *abhyudaya* (prosperity), while liberation (*mokṣa*) is considered *naiḥśreyasa* (the supreme good).
In brief, the summary of the means for this consists of faith and wisdom. Through faith one practices the Dharma; through wisdom one understands it according to reality.
Of these two, wisdom is the primary factor, yet faith is its precursor.
He who does not transgress the Dharma out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion should be known as one possessed of faith; he is the supreme vessel for the highest good.

He who, having thoroughly examined all actions of body, speech, and mind, and having understood what is beneficial for himself and others, always acts accordingly— he is a wise person. Non-violence, abstaining from theft, and avoiding the wives of others;
Restraint regarding false speech, slander, harsh words, and frivolous chatter;
the avoidance of greed, malice, and nihilistic views—these are the ten white paths of action; the black ones are the opposite.
Abstaining from intoxicants, a righteous livelihood, non-violence, giving with reverence,
honoring those worthy of honor, and loving-kindness— in brief, this is the Dharma.
For there is no Dharma derived solely from the mortification of the body.

He enters for a very long time the terrible wilderness of saṃsāra, where sentient beings are its trees and whose limbs are bitten by the serpents of the afflictions.
Through killing one is born short-lived; through violence, one suffers many ailments.
Through theft, one becomes addicted to sensual enjoyments; through sexual misconduct with another's wife, one becomes fearful.
From false speech comes rejection; from malicious speech, the alienation of friends;
from harsh speech, hearing what is unpleasant; and from idle chatter, ill-fortuned speech.
Covetousness destroys one's desires; malice is said to bring fear;
wrong view leads to false perspectives; and the drinking of intoxicants causes the delusion of the intellect.
Through non-giving comes poverty; through a wrong livelihood comes deception.
Through arrogance one attains birth in a low family; through envy, a lack of majesty;
through anger, an ugly complexion; and through failing to question the wise, stupidity.
These are the fruits within the human state, and prior to all of these, there is an evil rebirth.
The ripening that has been proclaimed for these things called unwholesome,
and for all wholesome things, is the arising of results in the opposite manner.
Greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the action born from them, are unwholesome.
Non-attachment, non-delusion, and non-hatred, as well as the action arising from them and its opposite, are auspicious.
From the inauspicious come all sufferings and likewise all miserable rebirths;
from the auspicious come all happy rebirths and all happinesses of birth.
The constant turning away from all that is unwholesome and the engagement in what is wholesome through mind,
action, and speech— this is remembered as the twofold Dharma.
By means of this Dharma, one is liberated from the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Among humans and gods, one attains the expansion of happiness, prosperity, and sovereignty;
through the meditations, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments, one enjoys the bliss of Brahmā and the other [deities].
Such, in brief, is this dharma of exaltation and its fruit.
Furthermore, the Dharma leading to the supreme good is subtle and profound in its vision;
it causes fear when taught to the foolish who lack the ear [of wisdom] by the Victors:
"I do not exist, nor shall I exist; nothing belongs to me, nor shall anything belong to me."

Thus, for the fool there is terror, while for the wise man there is the destruction of fear. This progeny, born of the notion of "I" and accompanied by the notion of "mine," has been declared as a mere wasteland by the one who speaks solely for the welfare of living beings.
"I exist" and "mine exists"— this is false from the perspective of ultimate reality,
because through the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are, neither of these two arises.
The aggregates arise from the conceit of "I," and that conceit of "I" is unreal in its objective sense.
For one whose seed is false, how could there be growth from truth?
(RATNA_01.29) Having thus seen the aggregates as unreal, ego-grasping is abandoned;
and through the abandonment of ego-grasping, there is no further arising of the aggregates. (RATNA_01.30)
Just as the reflection of one's own face is seen by depending upon a mirror,
yet that reflection is not anything at all in reality,
so too the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is perceived by depending upon the aggregates (*skandhas*).
And yet, that person does not exist in reality, like a reflection of one's own face.
Just as the reflection of one's own face is not seen without taking up a mirror,
so too [the self is not seen] without the aggregates.
"Even the notion 'I am' is not to be grasped.
Having heard such a teaching, the noble Ānanda attained the eye of Dharma and himself repeatedly declared it to the monks.
As long as there is grasping at the aggregates, so long is there the notion of "I.
When there is the ego-conception (*ahaṃkāra*), there is further karma, and from that, further birth. This threefold path—without beginning, middle, or end—is the circle of saṃsāra.
Resembling a whirling circle of fire, it revolves with mutual causality.
Since it is not obtained from itself, from another, from both, or even across the three times, the ego-conception perishes; and with that, karma and birth likewise perish.
Thus, seeing the arising of cause and effect as well as their cessation,
one does not, in reality, fall into the views of non-existence or existence regarding the world.
Having heard this Dharma which brings about the destruction of all suffering, the unexamining person—
One trembles due to lack of full understanding, being terrified of that which is not a ground for fear.
This entire [world] will not exist in nirvāṇa; you have no fear of this.
When its non-existence is spoken of here, how can it be terrifying to you?

In liberation there is neither self nor aggregates; if such liberation is dear to you, why is the removal of the self and the aggregates unpleasant to you right here? Nirvana is not even a non-existence, so how could it possibly have the nature of existence?

The exhaustion of the conceptualization of existence and non-existence is called nirvāṇa. In brief, the view that [the self] does not exist and that there is no fruit for action is known as the demeritorious, ruinous wrong view.
From the perspective of synthesis, there is the view that things exist, and that the fruits of actions exist;
right view is remembered as being meritorious and having a good rebirth as its natural outflow.
In knowledge, because existence and non-existence are stilled, there is the transcendence of both sin and merit.
Therefore, the wise declare that liberation is freedom from both this miserable state and this happy state.
Seeing arising together with its cause, one transcends non-existence;
one does not fall into existence either, seeing cessation together with its cause.
A cause that is prior-born or simultaneously born is, in reality, no cause at all;
for it is not established through conventional designation, and because it does not arise in terms of ultimate reality,
just as "short" exists only when "long" exists.
From its arising, this arises, just as light does from the arising of a lamp.
Furthermore, when "short" is absent, "long" does not exist by way of intrinsic nature;
since the lamp itself has not arisen, the light also cannot come to be.
Thus, seeing the arising of cause and effect, one does not fall into nihilism;
having accepted this world as it truly is, born of conceptual proliferation (prapañca),
and having approached the cessation of that which arises from proliferation according to reality.
Therefore, existence does not approach; thus, one who relies on non-duality is liberated.
(1.51) A form perceived from afar is seen clearly by those nearby.
If a mirage were water, why would it not be seen by those nearby? (1.52)

Just as this world is seen by those who have moved far away as it truly is, so it is not seen by those nearby; it is signless, like a mirage. Just as a mirage resembles water but is not water in reality, [so too is this world].

The aggregates are like the self; they are not the self, nor do they exist in reality. If one has come here thinking that a mirage is water, yet perceives that "this water does not exist," that person is truly a fool.
For one who grasps at this world, which is like a mirage, thinking "it exists" or even "it does not exist," this is delusion; and as long as there is delusion, one is not liberated. (RATNA 01.56)
The nihilist goes to an evil rebirth, while the believer goes to a happy rebirth;
through the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are, one who relies on non-duality attains liberation.
Not desiring either non-existence or existence, by means of the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are—

Through delusion, one attains non-existence; why does one not attain existence? (58) If, by refuting its existence, non-existence is implied by implication, why is existence not likewise implied simply by refuting non-existence? (59)
Since they have no thesis, no practice, and no mind, because they rely upon awakening—
how can those who are in fact nihilists in their meaning be considered nihilists?
[This applies to] those who propound the Sāṃkhya, Ulūka, Nirgrantha, the person (pudgala), and the aggregates (skandha).
Ask the world if it speaks of the transcendence of "is" and "is not. Know that this transcendence of existence and non-existence is the dowry of the Dharma;
it is called the profound nectar of the Buddhas' teaching.
It does not pass away, it does not come, nor does it remain for even a moment;
since its nature transcends the three times, how can the world exist in reality?
For both [the past and future], there is no coming, going, or staying in truth.
Therefore, what distinction can there be in reality between the world and nirvāṇa?
Since there is no abiding, there is neither arising nor cessation in truth;
how, then, could there be anything that has arisen, abides, or ceased in reality?
If an entity is non-momentary, how could there be transformation at all times?
If there is no transformation, from what source would there be change in reality?
[4b] Alternatively, it would have to be momentary either through the destruction of one part or through total destruction.
And because no irregularity is perceived, both [positions] are likewise illogical:
RATNA_01.67 If everything were momentary, how could there be any antiquity?
And even if it were non-momentary due to stability, how could there be any antiquity? RATNA_01.68
Just as a moment has an end, so too should its beginning and middle be conceived;

since a moment consists of these three parts, the world does not endure for even a single moment. Furthermore, the beginning, middle, and end must likewise be analyzed as being like moments themselves.
Neither from itself nor from another does [an entity] possess beginning, middle, or end.
It is not one, because it occupies multiple locations; nor is there anything that is without location.
Without the one, there is no many; and without existence, there is no non-existence either.
The non-existence of existence would result either from its destruction or from its counteragent;
yet how could there be destruction or a counteragent, since existence is impossible?
Therefore, in reality, the world does not undergo diminution through its cessation.
When asked whether the world is finite, the Jina remained silent.
It is by this very fact that the wise understand him to be omniscient—
that he did not speak of the profundity of this Dharma to a world that was not a fit vessel.
Thus, this dharma leading to the supreme good— profound, free from grasping,
and without abode— has been proclaimed by the perfectly awakened ones who perceive reality.
Because of this dharma that is without abode, people delight in having an abode.
Those of little intelligence, failing to transcend the notions of "it exists" and "it does not exist," perish in fear.
Having perished themselves, they cause others to perish, being terrified of that which is truly a state of fearlessness.
O King, act in such a way that you do not cause destruction by means of those who are themselves destroyed.
